title: Thanking your teachers
hook: the tradition owes honor to anyone who taught you even one letter
tomorrow: Rabbi Tarfon was in a hurry. so why say you needn't finish?

segments.voice: Last week ended turning the sources: turn it, and turn it again. The sources stay. This week, the people who handed them to you.
screen: `THE SOURCES STAY.` → `THE PEOPLE WHO HANDED THEM ON.`

segments.voice: A stack of thank-you cards on Noa's desk, most of them done. One is still blank: her drama teacher. Freshman year he put her in the chorus and told her she rushed every line. She was furious for a month. He taught her exactly two things: slow down, and listen to the other actor. She's used both in every show since. Does a teacher like that get a card? An old king had the same question, and his was much worse. David is walking up the Mount of Olives, weeping, barefoot, his head covered, running from his own son's revolt. Then the news reaches him. His trusted counselor, Ahithophel, has gone over to the other side.
screen: `ONE CARD STILL BLANK.` → `SLOW DOWN; LISTEN.` → `DAVID, BAREFOOT, WEEPING.` → `HIS COUNSELOR HAS GONE OVER.`

segments.voice: David prays that Ahithophel's advice will come to nothing, and in the story it does. You'd expect that to be the last word on the man. But Pirkei Avot remembers something else. It says David learned only two things from Ahithophel, and still called him my teacher, my guide, my close friend, words the sages read in a psalm of David. Two things, from a man who betrayed him. And from that the Mishnah draws a rule: whoever learns from another person a single chapter, a single law, a single verse, a single word, even a single letter, owes them honor. Even a single letter. That's the detail to tell someone tonight: in this tradition, the honor isn't measured by how much you were taught, or by how kind the teacher was. It's owed for the letter itself. So look back over these five years and you'll find teachers everywhere: parents, grandparents, a friend who explained a holiday, a sage dead for centuries, a stranger whose one sentence stuck. Some taught you a whole book. Some taught you one letter. All of them count.
screen: `ONLY TWO THINGS, FROM A TRAITOR.` · `STILL CALLED HIM MY TEACHER.` · `EVEN A SINGLE LETTER.` · `TEACHERS EVERYWHERE.` · then, large: `THANK THE TEACHERS.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one person who taught you something that stuck, even one small thing, even someone it's complicated to thank. Write them a message now, on paper or on your phone: the one thing they taught you, and thank you. Send it if you want to. Writing it is the practice.
screen: `ONE TEACHER, EVEN A HARD ONE.` · `THE ONE THING THEY TAUGHT YOU.` · `THANK YOU.`

segments.voice: Thanking your teachers: honor owed to anyone who taught you even one letter, the way David honored a teacher of two things.
Keep this: thank the teachers, even the ones who taught you one letter. Nine of fourteen.

howItsDone: Jewish tradition honors teachers highly; Pirkei Avot teaches that anyone who taught you even a single letter is owed honor, and students traditionally thank and honor their teachers for life.

Ahithophel.meaning: King David's counselor, who joined Absalom's revolt

Mount of Olives.meaning: the hill just east of Jerusalem

Pirkei Avot.meaning: a Mishnah tractate of the sages' sayings

Mishnah.meaning: the early code of Jewish law, the base of the Talmud

sources.ref: Pirkei Avot 6:3 (one who learns from another even a single letter must honor him; David and Ahithophel)

notes: Avot 6:3 paraphrased; the 'my teacher, my guide, my close friend' line is the sages' reading of Psalm 55:14 (JPS 1917 numbering), given in my words, not quoted.
2 Samuel 15:30 (weeping, barefoot, head covered) and 15:31 (David's prayer against Ahithophel's counsel) paraphrased; 17:14 shows the counsel defeated.
Chapter 6 of Avot (Kinyan Torah) is a later addition to the Mishnah; the script calls it Pirkei Avot and 'the Mishnah' loosely; Keeper may prefer 'the sages'.
'These five years' refers to the app's own path, not a claim.
Surprising fact: David honored a teacher who betrayed him, for two things learned.
